_about: Pre/post concept test for Module 3 (ADME). 'answer' is the index of the correct option. Check the science before using with students.

questions.q: What do the letters ADME stand for?
questions.why: ADME describes what the body does to a drug: it is absorbed, distributed, metabolised and excreted.

questions.q: A compound binds its target very strongly in the lab but fails in animals because almost none of it reaches the blood. Which ADME property is the most likely problem?
questions.why: Strong binding does not matter if the compound never reaches the target. Poor solubility or permeability limits absorption.

questions.q: In the BOILED-Egg style map, what does a compound inside the white region suggest?
options: Good passive absorption from the gut
The compound has a high molecular weight
It will bind strongly to every protein
questions.why: The white of the egg marks the TPSA and cLogP range where passive absorption through the gut wall is likely. The yolk adds likely passage through the blood-brain barrier.

questions.q: Which pair of properties draws the egg map?
options: Molecular weight and number of rings
questions.why: Too polar (high TPSA) and the drug cannot cross membranes; too greasy and it may not dissolve. The egg shows the balance.

questions.q: Aspirin is a weak acid (pKa about 3.5). In the stomach (pH about 1.5), most of it is…
options: Un-ionised, so it crosses membranes more easily
Ionised, so it cannot cross membranes
questions.why: When the pH is below the pKa of an acid, most of the acid keeps its proton and is neutral. Neutral molecules cross membranes more easily.

questions.q: What does phase I metabolism usually do to a drug?
options: Adds or reveals a polar group, for example by oxidation (often by CYP enzymes)
Attaches a sugar to make it excretable
questions.why: Phase I reactions (oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis) change the molecule. Phase II then conjugates it, for example with glucuronic acid.

questions.q: A drug has a half-life of 6 hours. About how long until it is almost completely removed (about 5 half-lives)?
questions.why: After one half-life half remains, then a quarter, an eighth and so on: after 5 half-lives about 3% is left, so about 5 × 6 = 30 hours.

questions.q: What happens if you take doses more often than the body can clear them?
options: The drug accumulates until it reaches a steady state (and may become toxic)
questions.why: Each dose adds to what is left from the last one. Levels rise until the amount removed in an interval equals the dose; if that is too high, the drug can be toxic.

options: Part of an oral dose is metabolised in the gut wall and liver before it reaches the general circulation
The first dose given to a patient
The first test of a compound in the lab
questions.why: Blood from the gut goes to the liver first. Drugs that are broken down there have a low oral bioavailability.

questions.q: Why are computational ADME predictions used early in a drug project?
options: They cheaply flag compounds likely to fail, so lab work focuses on better candidates; but they still need confirmation
They replace all animal and human studies
They prove a compound is safe
They are more accurate than experiments
questions.why: Predictions are fast and cheap guides. They reduce late failures but cannot replace experimental ADME and safety studies.
